analysis.one_liner: Extends pension and health plan protections to part-time, temporary, and contracted workers.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it sat in the House Education and Labor Committee and its Labor-Management Relations Subcommittee until the Congress ended, with no votes taken and no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Under federal pension law at the time, employees who worked fewer than 1,000 hours a year — roughly anyone working under about 20 hours a week — could be kept out of pension plans entirely. This bill would have treated 500 hours a year as enough to count toward pension participation, vesting, and benefit accrual, so part-time workers could earn retirement benefits. It also would have limited how much employers could cut the health insurance premium they pay for part-time workers, and would have counted long-term contracted and leased workers — people doing employee-like work but formally employed through staffing agencies or contractors — as employees for pension and health plan purposes.
analysis.who_benefits: Part-time and temporary workers earning pensions they otherwise could be excluded from; part-time workers whose employers would otherwise be free to slash the employer share of health premiums; and long-term contracted or leased workers who perform employee-like work but are formally employed by a middleman.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends ERISA so that employees working 500 or more hours a year (but under the 1,000-hour threshold that let employers exclude them) count toward pension participation, vesting, and benefit accrual rules. In practice, this meant a part-time worker putting in about 10 hours a week would start earning credit toward a pension instead of being shut out of the plan. [S2] [S3]

It restricts how far an employer can reduce the premium it pays for a part-time worker's group health coverage: a reduction is allowed only for employees customarily working under 30 hours a week, and even then the employer's contribution cannot fall below a proportional share of what it pays for a 30-hour-per-week employee. [S2] [S3]

It expands ERISA's definition of 'employee' to include people who provide employee-type services to an employer under contract or through leasing arrangements for at least a year at 500 or more hours a year (six months for core health benefits), bringing agency and contract workers into pension and health plan protections. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Employers maintaining pension and group health plans would bear added costs — pension accruals and vesting credit for part-time workers, higher health premium contributions for part-timers, and coverage of long-term contracted workers — and businesses that rely heavily on part-time, temporary, or outsourced labor would bear the most.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers using part-time and temp labor

drawbacks.text: The bill raises the cost of employing part-time, temporary, and contract workers. Employers facing those added costs could respond by cutting hours below the 500-hour threshold, converting positions to true independent contracts outside the law, or hiring fewer part-timers — a tradeoff the bill text itself does not address. [S3]

Plan sponsors and benefits administrators would face new compliance work: the bill requires fact-specific, plan-by-plan determinations of what 'positions' customarily involve fewer than the relevant hours, which Labor Department regulations would have to untangle. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change — letting someone working 10 hours a week earn pension credit — addresses a genuine gap in federal benefits law that pushed retirement risk onto workers with unpredictable hours. The costs fall on employers, and some could respond by restructuring work to keep people under the thresholds, which would blunt the benefit. The bill never advanced far enough for Congress to weigh these tradeoffs in hearings or amendment, so the design questions were never tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and then to its Labor-Management Relations Subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended — no hearings, no vote, no floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. Patricia Schroeder introduced the Part-Time and Temporary Workers Protection Act of 1989 on June 6, 1989. [S1] [S5]
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the day it was introduced. [S5]
On July 12, 1989, it was referred to the committee's Subcommittee on Labor-Management Relations, where the action record ends. [S5]
The bill drew no cosponsors, and the Congress ended on January 3, 1991, without the bill ever being reported out of committee or voted on. [S4] [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that rely on part-time, temporary, and contracted labor are better off, because the bill that would have required them to extend pension and health plan benefits to those workers died in subcommittee without a single cosponsor or hearing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers of part-time and temp labor

for.name: Rep. Patricia Schroeder
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 6, 1989; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never reported it out; it was sent to a subcommittee and no markup or vote was ever scheduled.

against.name: Subcommittee on Labor-Management Relations
against.role: Subcommittee of referral, House Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from July 12, 1989 until the Congress ended without action.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough for a partisan vote; its sponsor was a Democrat, it drew no cosponsors of either party, and no floor or committee votes were recorded. [S4] [S5]

industries.industry: Employers with part-time, temporary, and contract workforces (retail, food service, staffing agencies, outsourced services)
industries.note: The bill would have required them to extend pension and health plan benefits to workers they could previously exclude, raising labor costs. Businesses built on keeping hours low and workers formally off the payroll would have felt it most.

industries.industry: Employee benefits plan administrators and insurers
industries.note: More covered workers means more plans, more participants, and more administrative work under fact-specific hours rules. Insurers selling group health coverage could gain more premium volume from newly covered part-timers.
